extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literature; creative writers and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for judging poetry, drama, translation, and prose—covering originality vs. imitation, rhythm/readability, characterization, argumentative progression, and the relation of feeling to thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish promising craft from genuine genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic taste, dexterity in composition, and ingenious imitation often produce poems that are very promising in appearance. But genius, or the power of doing something new, is another thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that technical polish or attractive imitation guarantees lasting greatness; evaluate whether the work does something new rather than merely showing skill or resemblance to predecessors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry must have good sense and truth (plus imagination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is certainly something more than good sense, but it must be good sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poem should rest on intelligible, truthful perception even when it aspires to imagination or sublimity; translations or works lacking 'truth' or good sense may appear deficient in genuine poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of an idea matters more than prolixity
rubrics_metrics.description: Those enormously prolix harangues are a proof of weakness in the higher intellectual grasp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate prose and speeches by the clarity and presence of a central idea; verbosity or length without a clear idea indicates intellectual weakness rather than strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works should show genuine progression and development
rubrics_metrics.description: All that is worth anything in the Diversions of Purley is contained in a short pamphlet-letter; then it was enlarged to an octavo, but there was not a foot of progression beyond the pamphlet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A substantial work should advance, develop, or deepen its argument or subject beyond its initial formulations; mere enlargement without new substance is a flaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid shallow or unfair criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: His abuse of Harris is most shallow and unfair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical attacks should be substantive and proportionate; unfair polemic or superficial dismissal undermines the critic's credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: To criticize an institution, first understand its use
rubrics_metrics.description: No man can rightly apprehend an abuse till he has first mastered the idea of the use of an institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective critique demands comprehension of an institution's purpose and functioning before identifying or judging its abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate poetic originality by comparative subtraction
rubrics_metrics.description: No one can understand Shakspeare's superiority fully until he has ascertained, by comparison, all that which he possessed in common with several other great dramatists of his age, and has then calculated the surplus which is entirely Shakspeare's own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative analysis to distinguish an author's unique contributions from qualities shared with contemporaries; identify the 'surplus' that constitutes originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish authorial subjectivity from dramatic persona
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakspeare's poetry is characterless; that is, it does not reflect the individual Shakspeare; but John Milton himself is in every line of the Paradise Lost... I have no doubt whatever that Homer is a mere concrete name for the rhapsodies of the Iliad. ... There is no subjectivity whatever in the Homeric poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating narrative or dramatic works, decide whether the voice reflects the author's personal subjectivity, an adopted persona, or an impersonal collective tradition—this distinction affects interpretation and value judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess poetic force by how lines read aloud (rhythm and cadence)
rubrics_metrics.description: His rhythm is so perfect, that you may be almost sure that you do not understand the real force of a line, if it does not run well as you read it. The necessary mental pause after every hemistich or imperfect line is always equal to the time that would have been taken in reading the complete verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read lines aloud to judge their rhythmic power and natural pauses; a line's force is revealed in its spoken cadence and the reader's instinctive pauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use paradox and contradictory conceptions to gesture at higher truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato's works are preparatory exercises for the mind. He leads you to see, that propositions involving in themselves contradictory conceptions, are nevertheless true; and which, therefore, must belong to a higher logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that some philosophical or poetic truths may be expressed as apparent contradictions; such rhetorical or conceptual tension can be a deliberate device to indicate ideas beyond ordinary categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character delineation should show consistent traits and moral complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: How wonderfully beautiful is the delineation of the characters of the three patriarchs in Genesis!... Jacob is a regular Jew, and practises all sorts of tricks and wiles... Jacob is always careful not to commit any violence; he shudders at bloodshed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong characterization combines distinct, consistent traits with moral nuance; characters gain credibility when their actions and dispositions cohere across situations and reflect cultural-historical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: To persuade intellect, first arouse feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The best way to bring a clever young man, who has become sceptical and unsettled, to reason, is to make him feel something in any way. Love, if sincere and unworldly, will, in nine instances out of ten, bring him to a sense and assurance of something real and actual; and that sense alone will make him think to a sound purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In rhetoric and creative writing, evoking genuine feeling can be a precondition for eliciting sound thought or belief; craft should aim to engage emotion to open intellectual receptivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not trivialize a subject by turning it into political squibbery
rubrics_metrics.description: It shows a base and unpoetical mind to convert so beautiful, so divine, a subject as language into the vehicle or make-weight of political squibs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain respect for the intrinsic dignity of a subject; avoid reducing serious scholarly or aesthetic topics to partisan ridicule or cheap satire.
